prompt: What is a model's context window?
hint: Lesson 2: what does the application send with each request?

choices.text: The most tokens a request holds, reply included
choices.why: Right. The instructions, the history, the new input and the reply all share it.

choices.text: Everything the model remembers from your earlier chats
choices.why: It remembers nothing between requests. The window is what one request can carry.

choices.text: The part of the conversation the screen shows
choices.why: The screen has nothing to do with it. The window is counted in tokens, per request.

choices.text: How long the model takes to answer
choices.why: It is a size, not a time: a number of tokens.

prompt: `toylm generate "on sunday the café opens at" --temperature 0` wrote `seven.`, although the corpus says the café opens at eight on Sunday. Why?
hint: Read the context line of `toylm next`.

choices.text: The corpus never mentions Sunday
choices.why: It does, twice: `the café opens at eight on sunday`.

choices.text: Temperature 0 makes the model skip words it has seen rarely
choices.why: Temperature 0 picks the highest score. The scores came from `opens at` alone.

choices.text: Seven is the correct opening time on Sundays
choices.why: The corpus says eight on Sunday. The model never saw that the question was about Sunday.

choices.text: Its window held `opens at` and nothing more
choices.why: Yes. `sunday` was the fifth word from the end, outside the window, so it had no effect on the answer.

prompt: In the `grep` of the corpus, how many lines say the café opens at seven?
hint: Read the count in front of each line.

prompt: Which of these take up room in the context window of a request? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The system prompt
choices.why: Yes. It is sent with every request and counts every time.

choices.text: The earlier turns of the conversation
choices.why: Yes, both sides, because the application sends them again.

choices.text: The reply the model is about to write
choices.why: Yes. The reply is written inside the same window, which is why a full input leaves no room.

choices.text: The text the model was trained on
choices.why: Training text shaped the model's weights. It is not sent with the request.

choices.text: Your chats in other windows of the same app
choices.why: Only what the application puts into this request counts.

prompt: A request's input fills almost all of the model's window. What happens to the reply?

choices.text: The model compresses the input by itself to make room for a full reply
choices.why: Nothing compresses the input. Whatever is sent is read as it is.

choices.text: It runs out of room and stops, and the API reports `length`
choices.why: Right. The reply shares the window with the input, and lesson 15 is about that finish reason.

choices.text: The provider stretches the window for that one request
choices.why: The window is a fixed property of the model.

choices.text: The reply is written into a separate window of its own
choices.why: There is one window. The reply is generated inside it, after the input.

prompt: Where should you read the size of a model's window?
hint: Sizes change between models and versions.

choices.text: In the provider's documentation for that model, with the page's date
choices.why: Yes. Read it for the model you use, and note when the page was written.

choices.text: Ask the model in a chat how big its window is
choices.why: A model's answer about itself is generated text, and it is easily out of date.

choices.text: In last year's list of popular models
choices.why: Sizes change between versions. A list from last year can be wrong today.

choices.text: Anywhere, since it is the same for all models
choices.why: It differs between models and versions.

prompt: When a conversation is too long for its budget, what decides which turns are left out?
hint: `tok fit` plays that part in the lesson.

choices.text: The model, while reading, skips the turns it finds least useful
choices.why: The model receives only what the program sent. It does not choose.

choices.text: The provider drops turns at random
choices.why: The rule is chosen by the application. The usual one drops the oldest turns first.

choices.text: The user, by deleting old messages on the screen
choices.why: Truncation happens without the user doing anything, and usually without telling them.

choices.text: A program, before the model sees anything
choices.why: Right. The model never knows what was dropped; it receives what is left.

prompt: `tok fit chat.json -b 120` kept 3 of 7 turns. How many tokens did it send?
hint: The last line of the output.

prompt: With a budget of 120, an assistant could recommend the carrot and walnut cake to Bruno. What went wrong?

choices.text: The model saw the allergy and ignored it
choices.why: It never saw it. Turn 1 was dropped before the request was sent.

choices.text: The system prompt was dropped
choices.why: All three runs kept the system prompt, 53 tokens.

choices.text: The turn where Bruno said he was allergic was one of the oldest, so it was dropped
choices.why: Yes. The rule is oldest first, and the important fact happened to be said first.

choices.text: The budget raised the temperature
choices.why: A token budget has nothing to do with temperature. It decides what is sent.

prompt: Why does `tok fit` keep the system prompt, whatever else it drops?
hint: What would the assistant lose without it?

choices.text: The system prompt is the shortest message
choices.why: At 53 tokens it is the longest message in the conversation.

choices.text: It holds the rules
choices.why: Right: what the assistant is for, how to reply, and that the kitchen uses nuts.

choices.text: An API refuses any request that has no system prompt in it
choices.why: That is not why. It is kept because it carries the instructions.

choices.text: It is the newest message
choices.why: It is the first message. Keeping it is an exception to dropping the oldest first.

prompt: Why is a chat application cutting the history quietly more dangerous than an API refusing a request that is too long?
hint: Which of the two would you notice?

choices.text: Nothing signals the loss; the reply reads normally
choices.why: Right. A refusal is an error somebody sees; a truncated request looks exactly like a normal one.

choices.text: Truncation costs more than an error
choices.why: A truncated request costs less. The danger is in the content of the reply.

choices.text: Truncation also deletes the messages from the user's screen
choices.why: The user still sees them. Only the request to the model is cut, which is why the user is surprised.

choices.text: The API's error message is written by the model
choices.why: An error is returned by the provider's software, and no reply is generated.

prompt: `tok fit` keeps the system prompt, then keeps turns starting from the ___ one and working backwards.
hint: The one the user just sent.

prompt: `chat-noted.json` added one sentence about Bruno to the system prompt. Cut to the same budget of 120, what changed?
hint: Compare the two `tok fit` runs at 120.

choices.text: No turn was dropped this time
choices.why: The same four turns were dropped.

choices.text: The request became cheaper
choices.why: It went from 98 tokens to 116. The note costs tokens on every request.

choices.text: The allergy turn was moved to the end of the conversation
choices.why: The turns are unchanged. The note is in the system prompt.

choices.text: The allergy survived in the part that is not cut
choices.why: Yes. The same four turns were dropped, and the fact moved to where truncation does not reach.

prompt: The system prompt grew from 53 tokens to 71 with the note. How many tokens does the note add to every request?
Your assistant answers questions from a long staff handbook. What does this lesson recommend sending with each question?

choices.text: The whole handbook, every time, so nothing is missing
choices.why: That pays for every page on every request, and buries the line that answers among the others.

choices.text: Only the passages that match the question
choices.why: Right. The rest costs tokens and is text the model has to read past.

choices.text: A summary of the handbook written once at the start
choices.why: A summary drops details, and the detail a question needs is often the one it left out.

choices.text: Nothing, since the model already knows the handbook
choices.why: It knows nothing about this café's handbook unless the text is in the request.

prompt: A study found models used information at the start and end of a long context better than in the middle. What follows for a prompt with many documents?
hint: Where does the most important material go?

choices.text: Put the instruction and the key material at the start or the end, and test other positions
choices.why: Right. Do not bury what matters, and check the result with the fact moved around.

choices.text: Use the biggest window available, since the model reads it all equally
choices.why: The finding is that it does not read it all equally.

choices.text: Put the most important document in the middle so it has context on both sides
choices.why: The middle is where information was used worst.

choices.text: Send each document twice
choices.why: That doubles the cost and still leaves copies in the middle.

prompt: Put the steps `tok fit` follows in order.
hint: It starts with the message it never drops.
items: Add older turns one at a time while they fit
Stop at the first turn that does not fit, and drop it and everything older

prompt: Match each strategy to the problem it deals with.
hint: The headings of the last section.

pairs.right: a detail said in a turn that is about to be dropped
material too large to paste into every request
a job that needs all of a document longer than the window

right_distractors: a reply drawn at too high a temperature
